In [[mathematics]], a [[prime number]] ''p'' is called a '''Chen prime''' if ''p''&nbsp;+&nbsp;2 is either a prime or a [[semiprime|product of two primes]] (also called a semiprime). The [[even number]] 2''p'' + 2 therefore satisfies [[Chen's theorem]].

The Chen primes are named after [[Chen Jingrun]], who [[mathematical proof|proved]] in 1966 that there are [[Infinite set|infinitely]] many such primes. This result would also follow from the truth of the [[Twin prime|twin prime conjecture]] as the lower member of a pair of [[twin prime]]s is by definition a Chen prime.

The first few Chen primes are
:[[2 (number)|2]], [[3 (number)|3]], [[5 (number)|5]], [[7 (number)|7]], [[11 (number)|11]], [[13 (number)|13]], [[17 (number)|17]], [[19 (number)|19]], [[23 (number)|23]], [[29 (number)|29]], [[31 (number)|31]], [[37 (number)|37]], [[41 (number)|41]], [[47 (number)|47]], [[53 (number)|53]], [[59 (number)|59]], [[67 (number)|67]], [[71 (number)|71]], [[83 (number)|83]], [[89 (number)|89]], [[101 (number)|101]], ... {{OEIS|id=A109611}}.

The first few Chen primes that are not the lower member of a pair of twin primes are

:2, 7, 13, 19, 23, 31, 37, 47, 53, 67, 83, 89, 109, 113, 127, ...  {{OEIS|id=A063637}}.

The first few non-Chen primes are

:43, 61, 73, 79, 97, 103, 151, 163, 173, 193, 223, 229, 241, ... {{OEIS|id=A102540}}.

All of the [[Supersingular prime (moonshine theory)|supersingular primes]] are Chen primes.

[[Rudolf Ondrejka]] discovered the following 3 × 3 [[magic square]] of nine Chen primes:<ref>{{Cite web |title=Prime Curios! 59 |url=https://t5k.org/curios/page.php/59.html |access-date=2023-12-13 |website=t5k.org}}</ref>

{{as of|2018|3}}, the largest known Chen prime is {{val|2996863034895}} × 2<sup>{{val|1290000}}</sup> − 1, with {{val|388342}} decimal digits. 

The sum of the [[multiplicative inverse|reciprocal]]s of Chen primes [[convergent series|converges]].{{cn|date=November 2019}}

==Further results==
Chen also proved the following generalization: For any even [[integer]] ''h'', there exist infinitely many primes ''p'' such that  ''p''&nbsp;+&nbsp;''h'' is either a prime or a [[semiprime]].

[[Ben Green (mathematician)|Ben Green]] and [[Terence Tao]] showed that the Chen primes contain infinitely many [[arithmetic progression]]s of length 3.<ref>[[Ben Green (mathematician)|Ben Green]] and [[Terence Tao]], Restriction theory of the Selberg sieve, with applications, ''[[Journal de Théorie des Nombres de Bordeaux]]'' '''18''' (2006), pp. 147–182.</ref> Binbin Zhou generalized this result by showing that the Chen primes contain arbitrarily long arithmetic progressions.<ref>Binbin Zhou, [https://www.impan.pl/shop/publication/transaction/download/product/82619 The Chen primes contain arbitrarily long arithmetic progressions], ''[[Acta Arithmetica]]'' '''138''':4 (2009), pp. 301–315.</ref>
